claims.source: Importantly, we found that the alpha-correlate of tastiness was predicted closely by taste-EA (ralpha-EA = −0.90, p<0.001) but not taste-AC (ralpha-tastiness = −0.70, p>0.05), with the taste-EA signal showing a more precise relationship compared to the taste-AC signal across time (z = 4.09, p<0.001; Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha power and model simulations, shown in Figure 4e

claims.claim: Regulation may operate in part by altering alpha frequency representations of tastiness attributes, and this modulation might occur in relationship to evidence accumulation rather than attribute construction.
claims.source: These results suggest that regulation may operate in part by altering alpha frequency representations of tastiness attributes, and that this modulation might occur in relationship to EA rather than attribute construction.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of correlations between alpha power and model-predicted signals

claims.claim: Alpha signal was sensitive to tastiness for different durations on trials where the participant responded quickly compared to trials where they responded slowly.
claims.source: Follow-up tests confirmed this hypothesis: we found that alpha signal was sensitive to tastiness for different durations on trials where the participant responded quickly compared to trials where they responded slowly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of alpha power in fast vs. slow trials, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b

claims.claim: Alpha signals at taste-sensitive channels showed a build-up of correlation with tastiness in NATURAL trials that peaked just before the time of response both when decisions were made quickly and when they were made slowly.
claims.source: As expected, we found that alpha signals at taste-sensitive channels (Figure 4c, top left) showed a build-up of correlation with tastiness in NATURAL trials that peaked just before the time of response both when decisions were made quickly and when they were made slowly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, d).
claims.evidence: Supported by response-locked analysis of alpha power, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, d

claims.claim: There was an additional significant correlation with healthiness in taste-sensitive channels prior to the response on slow trials in the NATURAL condition, but not on the fast trials.
claims.source: Intriguingly, this analysis also revealed an additional significant correlation with healthiness in taste-sensitive channels prior to the response on slow trials in the NATURAL condition, but not on the fast trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e, f).
claims.evidence: Supported by response-locked analysis of alpha power in fast vs. slow trials, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3e, f

claims.claim: Raw alpha signals in taste-sensitive regions did build gradually, peaking in the time before response, but they did not always reach a fully clear and consistent value.
claims.source: Although we found that raw alpha signals in this region did build gradually, peaking in the time before response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), they did not always reach a fully clear and consistent value, as might be predicted if these signals provided the final trigger for the motor response.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of raw alpha power, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: The alpha-correlate of tastiness shows patterns consistent with some form of evidence accumulation, but may represent an intermediate stage of EA based on value that is then passed on to other mechanisms that accumulate evidence for a particular motor response.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that, while the alpha-correlate of tastiness shows patterns consistent with some form of EA, it may represent an intermediate stage of EA based on value that is then passed on to other mechanisms that accumulate evidence for a particular motor response.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of alpha power results

claims.claim: In the HEALTH condition, alpha power in frontal and parietal-occipital channels was negatively correlated with healthiness from ~500–1000 ms after presentation of food.
claims.source: Notably, in the HEALTH condition, we again found significant effects restricted to alpha power in frontal and parietal-occipital channels (Figure 4b). Alpha power in these channels was negatively correlated with healthiness from ~500–1000 ms after presentation of food (t(49) = −2.96, p=0.005; alpha-correlate of healthiness; Figure 4c, top-right).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of alpha power data, shown in Figure 4b and 4c

claims.claim: The timing of the alpha-correlate of healthiness correlated with the predicted time course of the health-EA signal and, less so, to the health-AC signals.
claims.source: The timing of this signal correlated with the predicted time course of the health-EA signal (ralpha-EA = −0.95, p<0.001) and, less so, to the health-AC signals (ralpha-healthiness = −0.76, p=0.02) signals.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha power and model simulations

claims.claim: The time course of the alpha-correlate of healthiness was significantly more strongly correlated with the health-EA signal than the health-AC signal.
claims.source: The time course was significantly more strongly correlated with the health-EA signal than the health-AC signal (z = 4.17, p<0.001; Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlations, shown in Figure 4f

claims.claim: Alpha power during the NATURAL and DECREASE conditions was not significantly associated with healthiness.
claims.source: As might be expected from model predictions, alpha power during the NATURAL and DECREASE conditions was not significantly associated with healthiness, although the contrast of average bhealthiness for alpha power between HEALTH and DECREASE or NATURAL in these channels ~500–1000 ms post-food failed to reach significance.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant associations

claims.claim: There was no evidence that the differences in alpha-healthiness correlate across conditions correlated with individual differences in the change in model parameters for the healthiness weight.
claims.source: Unlike the alpha-tastiness correlate, we found no evidence that the differences in alpha-healthiness correlate across conditions correlated with individual differences in the change in model parameters for the healthiness weight.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationships

claims.claim: Theta power at channels over occipital and frontal areas was positively correlated with tastiness early in the trial (200–500 ms) in both HEALTH and DECREASE conditions independently.
claims.source: Strikingly, and in contrast to alpha power, which tracks tastiness in the NATURAL condition but not regulation conditions, we found a single pattern matching our significance criterion: theta power at channels over occipital and frontal areas was positively correlated with tastiness early in the trial (200–500 ms) in both HEALTH (t(49) = 3.46, p=0.005; Figure 5a, b, top left) and DECREASE (t(49) = 2.8, p=0.01; Figure 5a, b, top-right) conditions independently.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta power data, shown in Figure 5a and 5b

claims.claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness was larger compared to NATURAL in both HEALTH and DECREASE.
claims.source: This effect was also larger compared to NATURAL in both HEALTH (t(49) = 2.90, p=0.009; occipital channels) and DECREASE (t(49) = 2.28, p=0.03; occipital and left central channels) (Figure 5b, bottom).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta power differences, shown in Figure 5b

claims.claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness might represent a 'control' process responsible for reducing the influence of tastiness attribute representations on the evidence accumulation process.
claims.source: Given the early appearance of this signal compared to the alpha-correlate of tastiness, we speculated that it might represent a 'control' process, rather than a representation of the tastiness attribute per se. This control process might be responsible for reducing the influence of tastiness attribute representations (which we observed in ERP signals) on the EA process (observed in alpha oscillations).
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the timing and pattern of theta power results

claims.claim: Subjects with greater increases in the theta-correlate of tastiness between 200 and 500 ms showed greater decreases in the weight on tastiness.
claims.source: We found that subjects with greater increases in the theta-correlate of tastiness between 200 and 500 ms showed greater decreases in the weight on tastiness (Δwtastiness), and this was independently true for the contrast of both HEALTH (Pearson r = –0.36, p=0.01) and DECREASE (Pearson r = –0.29, p=0.04) vs. NATURAL (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between theta power changes and model parameter changes, shown in Figure 5c

claims.claim: Changes in the alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness in DECREASE vs. NATURAL were correlated across subjects.
claims.source: Moreover, changes in the alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness in DECREASE vs. NATURAL were correlated across subjects (Pearson r = 0.43, p<0.001; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha and theta power changes, shown in Figure 5d

claims.claim: The more strongly tastiness was encoded in theta power early in the trial, the less strongly it was represented in the suppression of alpha power later in the trial.
claims.source: In other words, the more strongly tastiness was encoded in theta power early in the trial, the less strongly it was represented in the suppression of alpha power later in the trial.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between theta and alpha power changes

claims.claim: The relationship between changes in alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness was nonsignificant in the HEALTH condition.
claims.source: This relationship was nonsignificant in the HEALTH condition (Pearson r = 0.12, p=0.39; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationship, shown in Figure 5d

claims.claim: Event-related potentials correlated with the time course of model-predicted taste-attribute signals, with no modulation by regulation.
claims.source: Results suggested that event-related potentials (ERPs) correlated with the time course of model-predicted taste-attribute signals, with no modulation by regulation.
claims.evidence: Summary of results from ERP analysis

claims.claim: Suppression of frontal and occipital alpha power correlated with the time course of evidence accumulation, tracked tastiness according to its goal relevance, and predicted individual variation in successful down-regulation of tastiness.
claims.source: By contrast, suppression of frontal and occipital alpha power correlated with the time course of EA, tracked tastiness according to its goal relevance, and predicted individual variation in successful down-regulation of tastiness.
claims.evidence: Summary of results from alpha power analysis

claims.claim: An earlier rise in frontal and occipital theta power represented food tastiness more strongly during regulation and predicted a weaker influence of food tastiness on behaviour.
claims.source: Additionally, an earlier rise in frontal and occipital theta power represented food tastiness more strongly during regulation and predicted a weaker influence of food tastiness on behaviour.
claims.evidence: Summary of results from theta power analysis

claims.claim: Regulation modifies the representation of attributes during the process of evidence accumulation.
claims.source: Our findings illuminate how regulation modifies the representation of attributes during the process of EA.
claims.evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claims.claim: Suppression of alpha oscillations reflects active information processing involving release from inhibition, perception, and attention and appears to be driven by cortico-cortical networks across frontal and parietal brain regions.
claims.source: Suppression of alpha oscillations, also called the event-related desynchronization of alpha, is widely known to reflect active information processing involving release from inhibition, perception, and attention and appears to be driven by cortico-cortical networks across frontal and parietal brain regions (Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Klimesch et al., 2007; Samaha et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Klimesch et al., 2007; Samaha et al., 2018

claims.claim: The degree of alpha suppression predicts success in tasks where a higher level of cortical excitation is required.
claims.source: The degree of alpha suppression also predicts success in tasks where a higher level of cortical excitation is required (Klimesch et al., 2007), while inducing transient changes in alpha activity by external stimulation leads to predictable changes in cognitive performance (Klimesch et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Klimesch et al., 2007 and Klimesch et al., 2003

claims.claim: Prefrontal and posterior alpha suppression correlate with evidence accumulation in perceptual decision making.
claims.source: Other work also supports the idea that prefrontal and posterior alpha suppression correlate with EA, although such studies have focused on perceptual decision making (Kloosterman et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kloosterman et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014

claims.claim: Alpha suppression may relate to the control of cortical excitability in relation to accumulation of sensory evidence.
claims.source: This work suggests that alpha suppression may relate to the control of cortical excitability in relation to accumulation of sensory evidence (Kloosterman et al., 2019) in line with the proposed role for alpha in regulation of inhibition: increase in alpha power (synchronization) reflects inhibition and decrease in alpha power (desynchronization) reflects release from inhibition (Klimesch, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kloosterman et al., 2019 and Klimesch, 2012

claims.claim: Tastier foods may typically result in release from inhibition, potentiating approach-related responding, but this process is disrupted during regulation.
claims.source: One possibility, then, is that tastier foods may typically result in exactly this kind of release from inhibition, potentiating approach-related responding, but that this process is disrupted during regulation.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of alpha power results and known functions of alpha oscillations

claims.claim: Theta oscillations in the frontal cortex reflect cognitive control and integration of resources for cognitive control.
claims.source: Over the past several years, a consensus has emerged in the field that theta oscillations in the frontal cortex reflect cognitive control and integration of resources for cognitive control (e.g. Cavanagh and Frank, 2014; Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014; Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016

claims.claim: Midfrontal theta activates in response to any informative event or stimulus that conveys a need for behavioural adjustment or shift of attention.
claims.source: Midfrontal theta, in particular, activates in response to any informative event or stimulus that conveys a need for behavioural adjustment or shift of attention (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014) and recruits regions underlying different cognitive operations to realize this need for control (Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014 and Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016

claims.claim: Posterior theta oscillations may reflect the encoding of new information by the hippocampus in several memory operations.
claims.source: Posterior theta oscillations, on the other hand, may instead reflect the encoding of new information by the hippocampus in several memory operations (Axmacher et al., 2010; Klimesch, 1999; Scholz et al., 2017; Staudigl and Hanslmayr, 2013; Tesche and Karhu, 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Axmacher et al., 2010; Klimesch, 1999; Scholz et al., 2017; Staudigl and Hanslmayr, 2013; Tesche and Karhu, 2000

claims.claim: Early parietal and occipital theta oscillations correlate with value in high conflict choices and with cognitive load during mental calculation and multitasking.
claims.source: There is scattered evidence that early parietal and occipital theta oscillations correlate with value in high conflict choices (Hunt et al., 2012) and with cognitive load during mental calculation and multitasking (Wang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2018

claims.claim: Frontal theta in value-based decisions shows sensitivity to emotional stimuli and efficient sensory integration.
claims.source: On the other hand, frontal theta in value-based decisions also shows sensitivity to emotional stimuli and efficient sensory integration in different studies (Cavanagh et al., 2011; Nayak et al., 2019; Tosun et al., 2017; Zavala et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 2011; Nayak et al., 2019; Tosun et al., 2017; Zavala et al., 2016

claims.claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness may represent an inhibitory control mechanism that helps to gate the impact of the constructed attribute and prevent it from integrating into the processes reflected by alpha at frontal and posterior sites.
claims.source: This suggests that the theta-correlate of tastiness may represent an inhibitory control mechanism that helps to gate the impact of the constructed attribute that was reflected by front-central ERPS and prevent it from integrating into the processes reflected by alpha at frontal and posterior sites.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of theta power results and its relationship to alpha power

claims.claim: Previous perceptual decision-making studies have found that ERPs, in particular the P300 at centro-parietal electrodes, reflect the evidence accumulation process predicted by drift-diffusion model.
claims.source: While previous perceptual decision-making studies have found that ERPs, in particular the P300 at centro-parietal electrodes, reflect the EA process predicted by DDM (O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), our study found correlates of attribute values in ERPs with a more frontal distribution.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015

claims.claim: This is the first report to suggest a differentiation in the computational functions reflected by ERP and oscillatory signals during value-based choice.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this is the first report to suggest a differentiation in the computational functions reflected by ERP and oscillatory signals during value-based choice, although such distinctions have been previously reported in other cognitive processes (Hajihosseini and Holroyd, 2013; Holroyd et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Claim of novelty with reference to related work in other cognitive processes

claims.claim: Harris et al., 2013 reported an early attentional ERP component in occipital areas (N170) that was enhanced in successful self-control.
claims.source: For example, Harris et al., 2013 reported an early attentional ERP component in occipital areas (N170) that was enhanced in successful self-control and later centro-parietal ERP components localized to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that were sensitive to the overall value and tastiness and healthiness attributes.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2013

claims.claim: The early EEG predictors of regulation observed in this study as well as in Harris et al., 2013 might indicate a common oscillatory mechanism (occipital theta power) that controls the processing of attributes in the service of regulation.
claims.source: While a direct comparison of these two sets of findings is not possible due to differences in the study design and analysis, we speculate that the early EEG predictors of regulation observed in our study as well as in Harris et al., 2013 might indicate a common oscillatory mechanism (occipital theta power) that controls the processing of attributes in the service of regulation.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on comparison with prior work

claims.claim: The later components of attribute value represented by alpha suppression reflect the controlled integration of sensory evidence by areas involved in decision making and response selection.
claims.source: We also speculate that the later components of attribute value represented by alpha suppression in our study reflect the controlled integration of sensory evidence by areas involved in decision making and response selection.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of alpha power results

claims.claim: The study failed to replicate previous reports finding a distinct gamma (46–64 Hz) signature of value-based evidence accumulation at parietal and fronto-polar sites prior to response.
claims.source: Importantly, while we do observe neural signatures consistent with EA signals in our study, our results fail to replicate some previous reports in the literature finding a distinct gamma (46–64 Hz) signature of value-based EA (Polanía et al., 2014) at parietal and fronto-polar sites prior to response.
claims.evidence: Comparison with prior work showing non-replication

claims.claim: The study did not find a significant increase in gamma power in relation to the pre-food baseline in either food-locked or response-locked analysis.
claims.source: To test specifically whether we replicated this finding, we examined oscillatory power in the NATURAL condition averaged over all channels and specifically at Fz and Pz channels, but did not find an enhancement of gamma in relation to our pre-food 200 ms baseline (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a). To test whether this is due to higher variability in gamma phase in food-locked analysis, we also tested response-locked oscillatory power in relation to the pre-food baseline, but failed to find a significant increase in gamma power (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of gamma power shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: Discrepancies in gamma findings may be due to differences in the cognitive and memory demands presented by the different task paradigms.
claims.source: We speculate that these discrepancies may be due to differences in the cognitive and memory demands presented by the different task paradigms.
claims.evidence: Speculation about reasons for non-replication

claims.claim: Polanía et al., 2014 found that fronto-central low-beta (18–20 Hz) power was negatively correlated with evidence accumulation.
claims.source: In addition to gamma signals, Polanía et al., 2014 found that fronto-central low-beta (18–20 Hz) power was also negatively correlated with EA.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Polanía et al., 2014

claims.claim: The study observed suppression of low-beta power, though to a lesser degree compared to alpha power.
claims.source: Similarly, we also observed suppression of low-beta power (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), though to a lesser degree compared to alpha power.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: A full match to the single-trial value-based predictions of the drift-diffusion model regarding evidence accumulation only occurred with alpha suppression and did not match responses in the beta range.
claims.source: A full match to the single-trial value-based predictions of our DDM model regarding EA only occurred with alpha suppression (Figure 4e, f) and did not match responses in the beta range.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with alpha and beta power, shown in Figure 4e, f

claims.claim: Regulation reduces the behavioural influence of tastiness not by disrupting early, stimulus-locked representations of tastiness, but by using a theta-related regulatory mechanism to disrupt the incorporation of tastiness into alpha-related evidence accumulation processes.
claims.source: Taken together, our findings paint a nuanced portrait of the processes occurring during the regulation of value-based decision making. They suggest that regulation reduces the behavioural influence of tastiness not by disrupting early, stimulus-locked representations of tastiness, but by using a theta-related regulatory mechanism to disrupt the incorporation of tastiness into alpha-related EA processes.
claims.evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claims.claim: Alpha suppression may represent an identifiable signature indicating the integration of value-based attributes into the evidence accumulation process during both regulated and unregulated choices.
claims.source: Our findings corroborate previous accounts suggesting that alpha suppression tracks EA and further suggest that alpha suppression may represent an identifiable signature indicating the integration of value-based attributes into the EA process during both regulated and unregulated choices.
claims.evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claims.claim: Theta oscillations might play a role in inhibiting the influence of attribute values on evidence accumulation, independent of regulation strategy.
claims.source: Our study is also the first to our knowledge to find evidence that theta oscillations might play a role in inhibiting the influence of attribute values on EA, independent of regulation strategy.
claims.evidence: Claim of novelty based on the pattern of theta power results

claims.source: We recruited 66 participants from the University of Toronto Scarborough research participation system and flyers posted on campus.

claims.source: Participants were recruited until we obtained our pre-registered target sample size of 50 usable subjects (HajiHosseini and Hutcherson, 2020; https://osf.io/ewtvx/; 30 females, age range 17–31).
claims.evidence: Description of final sample size and demographics

claims.source: To increase motivation to eat, all participants were instructed to refrain from eating for 3 hr before the start of the experiment.
claims.evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claims.source: The experiment consisted of three tasks: a pre-choice rating task, a self-regulation choice task (SRCT), and a post-choice rating task (Hare et al., 2011; Harris et al., 2013; Hutcherson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Description of experimental design with citations to similar prior work

claims.claim: Recordings on Biosemi were sampled at 512 Hz, reference free, and later referenced to the averaged mastoids upon importing data to EEGLAB.
claims.source: Recordings on Biosemi were sampled at 512 Hz, reference free, and later referenced to the averaged mastoids upon importing data to EEGLAB (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).
claims.evidence: Description of EEG recording parameters with citation to EEGLAB

claims.claim: The drift-diffusion model included six parameters per condition: weights on tastiness, healthiness, a constant, decision threshold, starting point bias, and non-decision time.
claims.source: The DDM included six parameters per condition: three parameters related to drift rate (i.e. evidence/value formation) in each trial (weights on tastiness, wtastiness, healthiness, whealthiness, as well as a constant ValConst; total drift = wtastiness * tastiness + whealthiness * healthiness+ValConst), and three additional parameters: decision threshold (trs), starting point bias (spbias), and non-decision time (ndt) representing post-stimulus perceptual and pre-response motor processes.
claims.evidence: Description of computational model structure

claims.claim: HDDM uses hierarchical Bayesian estimation to identify the best-fitting parameters simultaneously for individual subjects and on the group level.
claims.source: HDDM uses hierarchical Bayesian estimation to identify the best-fitting parameters simultaneously for individual subjects and on the group level, assuming individual subjects' parameters are drawn from the group distribution.
claims.evidence: Description of model fitting procedure

claims.claim: The average simulated posterior predictive response times were significantly correlated with the observed response times across subjects and conditions (mean r = 0.46).
claims.source: We also found that the average simulated posterior predictive response times were significantly correlated with the observed response times across subjects and conditions (mean r = 0.46; t(49) = 17.1, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: Model validation showing good fit to data

results.result: Regulation significantly affected behavioral responses in food choice. Subjects accepted foods less often in DECREASE compared to NATURAL and HEALTH conditions, while response times were slower in both HEALTH and DECREASE compared to NATURAL.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C10 provide clear statistical evidence (p<0.001 for acceptance rates, p=0.004 for response times) demonstrating that regulatory instructions altered both choice outcomes and decision speed. The effects are well-documented with appropriate statistical tests and show expected patterns of behavioral regulation.

results.result: Drift-diffusion modeling revealed that both regulatory strategies (HEALTH and DECREASE) decreased the weight on tastiness, while HEALTH specifically increased the weight on healthiness. DECREASE resulted in a non-specific decrease in value constant.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 present a coherent pattern of model parameter changes with strong statistical support (all p<0.001). The differential effects on tastiness vs. healthiness weights across conditions provide mechanistic insight into how regulation operates. Model validation (C92) confirms good fit to data.

results.result: Regulation affected decision threshold and non-decision time but not starting point bias, suggesting effects occur during post-stimulus processing rather than pre-stimulus preparation.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 show systematic effects on DDM parameters beyond drift rate, with appropriate statistical tests. The lack of starting point bias effects (C17) provides important evidence about the timing of regulatory effects. Results are internally consistent and well-supported.

results.result: Model simulations predicted distinct temporal dynamics for attribute construction versus evidence accumulation signals. Attribute signals peaked earlier (516-570 ms) than evidence accumulation signals (630-660 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 present model-based predictions with strong statistical support (p<0.001) showing temporal separation between attribute construction and evidence accumulation. These predictions provide testable hypotheses for interpreting neural data, though they rely on model assumptions.

results.result: Fronto-central ERPs correlated with tastiness in the NATURAL condition and matched the predicted time course of taste attribute construction better than evidence accumulation. This ERP signal was not modulated by regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 provide convergent evidence linking ERPs to attribute construction rather than evidence accumulation, with strong correlations (r=0.89 for taste-AC vs r=0.77 for taste-EA, z=2.55, p=0.005). The lack of regulation effects (C24, C27) is important but limits the functional interpretation of this signal.

results.result: An exploratory analysis revealed early ERPs (200-400 ms) in occipital channels correlated with healthiness in the HEALTH condition, but this signal did not correlate with behavioral regulation success.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 describe an exploratory finding that was not predicted by the model. While statistically significant (p=0.007), the lack of correlation with behavioral changes (C29) and the post-hoc nature of the analysis limit confidence in its functional significance.

results.result: Alpha power suppression in frontal and parietal-occipital channels correlated with tastiness only in the NATURAL condition (500-1000 ms post-food), was disrupted during regulation, matched the predicted time course of evidence accumulation better than attribute construction, and predicted individual differences in successful down-regulation of tastiness.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 provide strong convergent evidence linking alpha suppression to evidence accumulation of tastiness. The signal shows regulation-dependent modulation (C31-C32), matches EA predictions better than AC predictions (C34: z=4.09, p<0.001), and correlates with behavioral regulation success (C33: r=-0.28 to -0.29, p≤0.05). This is a key finding of the paper.

results.result: Follow-up analyses of alpha signals showed response-time dependent dynamics consistent with evidence accumulation, including build-up to response in both fast and slow trials, though signals did not always reach a fixed bound, suggesting an intermediate stage of value-based evidence accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 provide additional validation of the alpha-EA relationship through response-locked analyses. The findings are consistent with evidence accumulation (C37) but the lack of a clear fixed bound (C39) appropriately qualifies the interpretation (C40). The analyses strengthen confidence in the main result while acknowledging complexity.

results.result: In the HEALTH condition, alpha power in frontal and parietal-occipital channels was negatively correlated with healthiness (500-1000 ms), matched the predicted time course of health-related evidence accumulation, but did not correlate with individual differences in healthiness weight changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 show alpha correlates of healthiness with strong model correspondence (r=-0.95 for health-EA, z=4.17, p<0.001). However, the lack of correlation with behavioral changes (C45) and weaker condition-specificity (C44) suggest this signal may be less robust or functionally important than the tastiness correlate.

results.result: Theta power in occipital and frontal areas positively correlated with tastiness early in the trial (200-500 ms) specifically during regulation conditions, predicted greater decreases in tastiness weight, and was negatively correlated with alpha-correlate changes in DECREASE but not HEALTH.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 describe a novel theta signal that appears during regulation, predicts behavioral success (C49: r=-0.29 to -0.36, p≤0.04), and shows an inverse relationship with alpha changes (C50: r=0.43, p<0.001). While C48 is speculative, the overall pattern provides strong evidence for a regulatory control mechanism. The differential correlation pattern between DECREASE and HEALTH (C52) adds complexity.

results.result: Overall, ERPs correlated with attribute construction without regulation modulation, alpha suppression correlated with evidence accumulation and tracked goal-relevant attributes, and theta power represented a regulatory control mechanism, together illuminating how regulation modifies attribute representation during evidence accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 synthesize the main findings into a coherent framework. The distinct functional roles of ERPs, alpha, and theta are well-supported by the preceding analyses. This represents the core contribution of the paper, integrating computational modeling with neural dynamics.

results.result: The study failed to replicate previous findings of gamma (46-64 Hz) signatures of value-based evidence accumulation, finding no significant gamma power increase in either food-locked or response-locked analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 clearly document a non-replication with appropriate analyses. C75 offers speculation about task differences but this remains untested. The non-replication is important to report but the lack of gamma findings doesn't undermine the main alpha/theta results.

results.result: While low-beta (18-20 Hz) power suppression was observed, only alpha suppression fully matched single-trial value-based predictions of the drift-diffusion model for evidence accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide appropriate comparison with prior work and justify focus on alpha. The observation of beta suppression (C77) with weaker model correspondence (C78) helps validate the specificity of alpha findings.

results.result: The study concludes that regulation reduces tastiness influence not by disrupting early attribute representations but through theta-mediated disruption of tastiness incorporation into alpha-related evidence accumulation, with alpha suppression serving as a signature of attribute integration into evidence accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 present the main conclusions, which are well-supported by the convergent evidence from behavioral, modeling, ERP, alpha, and theta analyses. The mechanistic account is appropriately qualified and represents a significant advance in understanding dietary self-regulation.

results.result: The study recruited 66 participants, excluded 16 based on pre-registered criteria or technical issues, resulting in a final sample of 50 subjects (30 females, age 17-31) who fasted for 3 hours before the experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 document appropriate sample size determination, pre-registered exclusion criteria, and experimental controls. The final sample size of 50 meets the pre-registered target and provides adequate power for the main analyses.

results.result: The experiment used a three-task design (pre-rating, choice, post-rating) with 64-channel EEG recorded at 512 Hz and referenced to averaged mastoids.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 describe standard experimental and recording procedures appropriate for the research questions. The methods are clearly documented and follow established practices in the field.

results.result: The drift-diffusion model included six parameters per condition and was fit using hierarchical Bayesian estimation (HDDM), with model validation showing good correspondence between simulated and observed response times (r=0.46, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 document appropriate computational modeling procedures. The model validation (C92) provides important evidence that the model captures key aspects of the data, supporting the use of model-derived predictions for interpreting neural signals.

results.result: The introduction establishes theoretical background from prior work on value-based decision making, evidence accumulation, self-regulation, and EEG correlates of these processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 accurately summarize relevant prior work with appropriate citations. These claims establish the theoretical foundation and motivation for the current study. The characterizations of prior work appear accurate based on the citations provided.

results.result: The discussion interprets alpha suppression findings in the context of established literature on alpha oscillations reflecting release from inhibition, cortical excitability, and evidence accumulation in perceptual decision making.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 accurately characterize prior work on alpha oscillations with appropriate citations. C61 offers reasonable speculation about mechanisms linking alpha to approach behavior, though this remains to be tested. The interpretation is well-grounded in existing literature.

results.result: The discussion interprets theta findings in the context of literature on frontal theta reflecting cognitive control and posterior theta reflecting memory encoding, speculating that the observed theta-correlate represents an inhibitory control mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 accurately summarize relevant theta literature with appropriate citations. C67 offers reasonable speculation about the functional role of the observed theta signal, appropriately qualified as speculative. The interpretation is consistent with the data pattern.

results.result: The discussion compares findings to prior EEG work on value-based decision making, noting this is the first report of functional differentiation between ERP and oscillatory signals in value-based choice and speculating about relationships to prior findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 make appropriate comparisons to prior work and claim novelty that appears justified. C70-C72 offer reasonable speculation about relationships to prior findings (Harris et al., 2013), appropriately qualified given methodological differences. The novelty claim appears warranted.
